content.title: About
content.content: NOS is an energy drink designed to boost physical and mental performance. It contains caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins and sugar (or sugar substitutes in diet versions). The drink is popular among athletes and anyone needing a quick energy surge.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: NOS was first launched in 2005 as part of Monster’s energy‑drink lineup.
The original formula provides 160 mg of caffeine per 12 oz (355 ml), roughly the amount in two cups of coffee.
The brand heavily sponsors motorsports events, emphasizing its association with speed and adrenaline.
Sugar‑free versions are available in several markets, using artificial sweeteners to meet low‑calorie demands.
Taurine, one of the key ingredients, occurs naturally in meat and fish and is thought to support heart and muscle function.

items.title: Increased alertness
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving focus and reducing perceived fatigue.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: B‑vitamins (B6, B12, niacin) play a role in converting food into usable energy.

items.title: Enhanced physical endurance
items.content: Taurine may help muscles use oxygen more efficiently during intense exercise.

items.title: Antioxidant effect
items.content: Some formulations are fortified with vitamin C, which helps combat free radicals.

items.title: Excessive caffeine intake
items.content: High doses can cause anxiety, insomnia, rapid heartbeat, and elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The regular version contains about 27 g of sugar per can, which may contribute to weight gain and dental issues.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of certain stimulants and diminish the efficacy of some sedatives.

items.title: Not recommended for children and pregnant women
items.content: Due to high caffeine and taurine levels, these groups should limit or avoid consumption.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Consume one 12‑oz (355 ml) can 15–30 minutes before physical activity or when you need a rapid energy boost. Do not exceed 2–3 cans per day to avoid caffeine overload.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 24 hours.

turkey-light-meat-breaded-baked-or-fried.title: Turkey, light meat, breaded, baked or fried, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a North American bird whose white meat is tender and low in fat, especially when the skin is removed. When breaded and baked or fried, it stays juicy while the crust adds a crunchy texture. The skin, if left on, is edible and provides beneficial fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkeys were domesticated by indigenous peoples of Mexico over 2,000 years ago.
White turkey meat contains fewer calories than red meat but is rich in protein.
Breadings are often made from whole‑grain flour or breadcrumbs, increasing fiber content.
Baked turkey retains more B‑vitamins than fried turkey.
Turkey skin contains omega‑3 fatty acids when it is not removed.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: White turkey meat provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef or pork, turkey has less saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey is rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which aid metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc – nutrients important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Fiber in whole‑grain breading
items.content: Using whole‑grain breading adds dietary fiber that helps regular digestion.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat.

items.title: Sodium in pre‑made breadings
items.content: Commercial breading mixes often contain added salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Calorie density when fried
items.content: Fried breaded turkey can be higher in calories due to oil, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Like any raw poultry, turkey can harbor salmonella; it must be cooked to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breaded turkey can be baked in the oven until golden brown or pan‑fried with a little oil. Serve with vegetable sides, salads or whole‑grain grains. Leaving the skin on adds extra flavor and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw turkey in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days, and cooked dishes in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at ‑18 °C; thaw in the refrigerator before use.

vienna-sausages-stewed-with-potatoes-pue.title: Vienna Sausages Stewed with Potatoes, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Vienna sausages stewed with potatoes in Puerto Rican style is a dish where small canned sausages are combined with diced boiled potatoes in a savory tomato sauce flavored with onion, garlic, sweet pepper and typical Puerto Rican spices such as adobo and oregano.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish appeared in the mid‑20th century when American canned sausages became popular throughout the Caribbean.
Stewing the sausages in tomato sauce keeps them moist and adds a mild heat.
In Puerto Rico it is often served alongside rice and beans, forming the classic “combination” meal.
The sausages used are usually tiny (about 2–3 cm long), which helps them distribute evenly among the potatoes.
Tomatoes are frequently replaced with tomato paste to speed up cooking.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The sausages provide animal protein needed for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat products, including these sausages, are a good source of heme iron, which supports oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Potatoes – potassium source
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which helps maintain normal blood pressure and nerve function.

items.title: Tomatoes – antioxidants
items.content: Tomato‑based sauce supplies lycopene and vitamin C, both of which combat free radicals.

items.title: Mild spices
items.content: Adobo and oregano have anti‑inflammatory properties and can aid digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned sausages often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: The sausages can be relatively high in saturated fat, which should be limited in heart‑related conditions.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some brands use nitrites and other preservatives that can be harmful in excess.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: A minority of individuals may experience allergic reactions to sausage ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stew hot in a deep plate. It pairs well with boiled rice, beans, or crusty bread. Garnish with fresh cilantro, a squeeze of lime, or hot sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it remains good for up to 2 months after cooling and sealing in a freezer‑safe bag.
